changes.before: Build grouped form fields with native validation and helpful errors.
changes.after: Put related form fields in named groups.

before: A longer form becomes easier to understand when related fields have clear groups. fieldset groups controls, and legend names the group. Contact details and account details are different subjects, so they can use separate fieldsets in one form. People using assistive tools can receive the group name with the fields. Grouping does not save information or guarantee that an answer is correct. It makes the form's structure clearer. This exercise builds grouped registration fields; showing one step at a time would require additional navigation behavior.

This fragment belongs inside body. It creates one labeled group with native validation.

```html
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Participant details</legend>
    <label for="participant">Participant name</label>
    <input id="participant" name="participant" required>

    <label for="reply">Reply email</label>
    <input id="reply" name="reply" type="email" required>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
```

legend is the first child of fieldset and names the group. Each label points to a unique input id. required asks for an answer, and type="email" checks an address-shaped value. The input elements need no closing tags, while form, fieldset, legend, label, and button do.

Constraints are limits on acceptable input. required rejects a missing answer during ordinary submission. type="email" adds a format check. minlength sets a minimum text length. These work together, rather than replacing each other. A minlength field that is optional can still be empty, so add required when empty input should be rejected. type="password" hides entered characters visually; it does not by itself encrypt, store, or secure the value. Any real account system needs separate secure handling and server validation.

Helpful instructions appear before someone makes an error. Tell them the length requirement in words near the field. A small element marks side information such as a short note, not a particular font size you must rely on. aria-describedby can connect a control to explanatory text through that text's id. Unlike a label, the description gives extra help rather than naming the field. Keep the actual visible label. IDs must be unique, and both for and aria-describedby must point to the correct elements.

Add this fieldset inside the same form, before its submit button, to give the example a second group.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Account details</legend>
  <label for="secret">Passphrase</label>
  <input
    id="secret"
    name="secret"
    type="password"
    minlength="10"
    required
    aria-describedby="secret-help"
  >
  <small id="secret-help">Use at least ten characters.</small>
</fieldset>
```

The multi-line opening input tag is still one tag. The minimum here is ten, to show a different example. aria-describedby points to the help note. Nest this fieldset within form, and close it before the form closes.

Validate the paths someone can take. First submit with required fields blank. Next try an invalid email and a short passphrase. Then type valid-shaped information that meets the length rule. Browser validation normally prevents the ordinary submission while a participating field is invalid, and may focus it with a message. Test with typing, because programmatically changing values can behave differently for some constraints. Do not use a fake error that only says “Wrong”: say which field needs attention and what would make it acceptable. Native checks remain only part of a complete registration system.

For the workshop exercise, make exactly two fieldsets, each with a legend. Add labeled inputs for name, email, and passphrase, using the expected ids name, email, and pass. Require the needed fields, give email its email type, and give pass a minlength of at least eight. Keep a submit button. The checks verify groups, labels, and key constraints; they do not implement multi-step navigation or a database. Explain what each fieldset contains and test missing, invalid, and valid values with the keyboard before considering the form usable.
after: `<fieldset>` groups related fields. `<legend>` gives the group a name. A registration form can have one group for contact details and another for account details. Grouping helps people understand the form; it does not turn it into separate steps.

This group asks for contact details.

```html
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Participant details</legend>
    <label for="participant">Participant name</label>
    <input id="participant" name="participant" required>

    <label for="reply">Reply email</label>
    <input id="reply" name="reply" type="email" required>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
```

`<fieldset>` wraps the two fields. Its first child, `<legend>`, names the group. Each label points to its input’s id. The submit button stays outside the group but inside the form.

A constraint is a rule for an entry. `required` means it cannot be empty. `type="email"` checks the shape of an email address. `minlength` sets the shortest allowed text. Use `required` too if a short-text field must not be left blank.

Help text explains a field’s rule before someone types. Give the help text an id. Use that id in the field’s `aria-describedby` so a screen reader can connect the help to the field. Keep the visible label as well.

This second group belongs inside the same form, before its button.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Account details</legend>
  <label for="secret">Passphrase</label>
  <input
    id="secret"
    name="secret"
    type="password"
    minlength="10"
    required
    aria-describedby="secret-help"
  >
  <small id="secret-help">Use at least ten characters.</small>
</fieldset>
```

The legend names Account details. `minlength="10"` asks for at least ten characters in this example. `aria-describedby` points to the help note. `type="password"` hides the typed characters on screen; it does not make an account secure by itself.

Try the form by typing. First leave required fields empty. Next try an email without `@` and a short passphrase. Finally type values that meet the rules. The browser should help you find and fix invalid fields. This practice does not create an account.

Make two fieldsets: Contact details and Account details. Give each a legend. Add labeled inputs with ids `name`, `email` and `pass`, and give each a name. Require all three. Use email type for email and password type for pass. This task asks for a minimum of eight characters. Add help text for that rule and keep a submit button.

before: Group the fields in two fieldset elements. Give each group a heading with legend.
Add labels for name, email, and passphrase. Match each label’s for value to its field’s id.
Add required to all three fields.
Set the email field to type="email".
Set the passphrase field’s minlength to at least 8.
Try submitting blank fields, an email without an @ sign, and a passphrase shorter than eight characters. Then try valid details.
after: Create the contact and account fieldsets with legends.
Add the three labeled, required inputs and their rules.
Add passphrase help and a submit button, then run the checks.
Type missing, invalid and valid entries to try the form.

before.question: You group registration fields in a fieldset with a legend. Has this made their submitted values trustworthy?
choices: No; grouping names related controls, but the server still validates values
Yes; the legend validates all fields in its group
Yes; a fieldset prevents the browser checks being bypassed
before.explanation: fieldset and legend give structure and a group name. They do not validate or secure submitted data; server checks are still necessary.

after.question: Does a fieldset with a legend prove that the entered information is correct?
choices: No. It groups and names fields; the receiving service still needs checks.
Yes. The legend checks every entry.
Yes. Grouped fields cannot contain incorrect values.
after.explanation: A fieldset explains which fields belong together. It does not check or secure their values.

before: Fieldset groups controls; legend names the group.
Every input needs a unique id and matching label.
Use required, email type, and minlength="8".
after: Use exactly name, email and pass for the input ids.
Keep each legend first inside its fieldset.

project.title: Group related registration fields
project.task: Build two named field groups with required name, email and passphrase inputs.
project.done_when: There are two fieldsets with legends. All three inputs have labels and are required; email uses email type and pass has a minimum length of eight.
